Aortic dissection:
A 58-year-old male presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset, severe chest pain that started 30 minutes ago while resting. He describes the pain as tearing and ripping, radiating from the anterior chest to the back between the shoulder blades.

[b]Past Medical History:[/b]
• Long-standing uncontrolled hypertension
• Poor adherence to antihypertensive medications
• No previous cardiac surgery

• BP: 190/110 mmHg (right arm)
• BP: 155/90 mmHg (left arm) — note the inter-arm difference
• HR: 112 bpm
• RR: 24/min
• SpO₂: 96% on room air
• Temperature: 36.8°C

[b]Physical Examination:[/b]
• Patient appears anxious and diaphoretic
• Unequal radial pulses
• New early diastolic murmur suggestive of aortic regurgitation
• No obvious signs of heart failure

• [b]ECG:[/b] Sinus tachycardia, no ST-segment elevation
• [b]Troponin:[/b] Slightly elevated
• [b]Chest X-ray:[/b] Widened mediastinum
• [b]Bedside echocardiography:[/b] Dilated aortic root with suspected intimal flap
What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate immediate management strategy?

[b]A.[/b] Acute myocardial infarction (STEMI) → Immediate thrombolysis.

[b]B.[/b] Acute Type A Aortic Dissection → Immediate IV beta-blocker therapy followed by emergency cardiothoracic surgical evaluation and repair.

[b]C.[/b] Acute pulmonary embolism → Immediate IV anticoagulation with heparin.

[b]D.[/b] Hypertensive emergency → Immediate IV nitroglycerin without beta-blockade.

[b]E.[/b] Acute pericarditis → NSAIDs and colchicine.

The clinical presentation strongly suggests acute aortic dissection:

• [b]Sudden severe tearing chest pain[/b] — classic presentation of aortic dissection.
• [b]Radiation to the back[/b] — suggests involvement of the thoracic aorta.
• [b]Unequal blood pressure between arms[/b] — indicates aortic arch branch involvement.
• [b]Unequal radial pulses[/b] — suggests impaired flow due to dissection.
• [b]New diastolic murmur[/b] — suggests acute aortic regurgitation from aortic root involvement.
• [b]Widened mediastinum[/b] — an important radiological clue.
• [b]Intimal flap on echocardiography[/b] — strongly supports the diagnosis.

Stanford Type A dissection involves the ascending aorta, regardless of whether the dissection extends into the descending aorta.

It is a [b]surgical emergency[/b] because it can rapidly lead to:
• Aortic rupture and cardiac tamponade
• Acute severe aortic regurgitation
• Myocardial infarction
• Cerebral or visceral malperfusion
• Sudden death
WHY ARE THE OTHER OPTIONS INCORRECT?

[b]A. Acute MI (STEMI):[/b] ECG shows no ST elevation. Tearing pain, unequal pulses, unequal arm BPs, and widened mediastinum favor dissection. Thrombolysis in unrecognized dissection can cause fatal rupture.

[b]C. Pulmonary Embolism:[/b] PE presents with dyspnea and pleuritic pain — not unequal arm BPs, unequal pulses, or intimal flap. Anticoagulation before excluding dissection is dangerous.

[b]D. Hypertensive Emergency:[/b] Severe HTN is present but not the primary diagnosis. Vasodilators should not be started before beta-blockade (reflex tachycardia increases aortic wall stress).

[b]E. Acute Pericarditis:[/b] Sharp pleuritic pain that improves sitting forward. Does not explain pulse deficit, inter-arm BP difference, or intimal flap.

• Activate emergency and cardiothoracic surgery teams immediately
• Continuous ECG, BP, and SpO₂ monitoring
• Two large-bore IV lines
• Keep patient NPO
• Send CBC, renal function, electrolytes, coagulation profile, blood group, crossmatch
• Supplemental oxygen if hypoxemic
• Adequate IV analgesia — usually an opioid such as fentanyl

[b]First-line: IV Beta-blocker[/b]

[b]Esmolol:[/b]
• Loading: 500 mcg/kg IV over 1 minute
• Maintenance: 50–200 mcg/kg/min IV infusion, titrated

[b]Alternative — Labetalol:[/b]
• 10–20 mg IV initially
• Additional doses or infusion per BP and HR response

[b]Treatment Targets:[/b]
• Heart rate: 60–80 bpm
• Systolic BP: < 120 mmHg (or lowest maintaining organ perfusion)

• [b]CT angiography (CTA) of the aorta:[/b] Preferred in hemodynamically stable patients
• [b]Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE):[/b] Particularly useful when unstable or transport is unsafe

[b]For Stanford Type A dissection:[/b]
• Immediate cardiothoracic surgical consultation
• Emergency surgical repair of the ascending aorta
• Aortic valve repair or replacement if indicated

[b]NEVER give a vasodilator before controlling heart rate and contractility.[/b]

Reflex tachycardia from vasodilators can increase aortic wall stress and worsen the dissection.

In any patient with sudden severe tearing chest pain, especially with unequal arm BPs or pulse deficits:
• Suspect acute aortic dissection immediately
• Do NOT administer thrombolytics or anticoagulants reflexively
• Start IV beta-blocker first
• Activate cardiothoracic surgery without delay

• [b]Tearing chest pain radiating to the back:[/b] Think aortic dissection
• [b]Unequal arm BP:[/b] Consider aortic branch involvement
• [b]Pulse deficit:[/b] Suggests arterial malperfusion
• [b]New diastolic murmur:[/b] Consider acute aortic regurgitation
• [b]Widened mediastinum:[/b] Suspect aortic dissection
• [b]Pericardial effusion or tamponade:[/b] Consider aortic rupture

[b]Type A:[/b] Ascending aorta involved → [b]Emergency surgery[/b]

[b]Type B:[/b] Ascending aorta not involved → Usually initial medical management, with intervention for complicated cases

[b]The first minutes matter![/b]

In any patient presenting with sudden severe tearing chest pain, especially with unequal arm blood pressures or pulse deficits:

• Suspect acute aortic dissection immediately
• Do NOT administer thrombolytics or anticoagulants reflexively
• Start IV beta-blocker therapy (if not contraindicated)
• Control systolic BP while maintaining organ perfusion
• Arrange urgent CTA if stable
• For Type A dissection, activate cardiothoracic surgery immediately

[b]Remember: Type A = Surgical Emergency.[/b]
